paragraphs.title: Job’s Complaint of Injustice and Obstruction

answers: As words of comfort
As words that vex and break him
As words of praise
easy.explanation: Job says that they vex his soul and break him in pieces with words.
easy.q: How does Job describe his friends’ words to him?

answers: Fenced it up and made it impassable
Made it broad and pleasant
Filled it with light
easy.explanation: Job says God fenced up his way so that he cannot pass and set darkness in his paths.
easy.q: What does Job say God has done to his way?

answers: His house
His book
His glory and crown
easy.explanation: Job says that God stripped him of his glory and took the crown from his head.
easy.q: What has been taken from Job, according to his complaint?

answers: He says that even if he has erred, the error remains his own and does not justify their reproach
He admits every accusation against him
He says he cannot remember their words
medium.explanation: Job says, “mine error remaineth with myself,” distinguishing his possible error from their unjust treatment.
medium.q: Why does Job reject the charge that his error justifies their treatment of him?

answers: Opened widely
Blocked with a barrier
Decorated beautifully
medium.explanation: To fence up a way is to block or enclose it so that passage is impossible.
medium.q: In the phrase “He hath fenced up my way,” what does “fenced up” mean?

answers: He loses only his possessions
He loses honor, direction, hope, and safety as troubles surround him
He receives help from every side
medium.explanation: Job describes a blocked path, lost glory, removed hope, divine wrath, and troops encamped around his tabernacle.
medium.q: How do the signs of Job’s suffering accumulate in this passage?

answers: His hope has grown stronger
His hope has been uprooted or taken away
His hope has been hidden in a forest
challenge.explanation: The comparison to a removed tree pictures hope being forcibly uprooted.
challenge.q: What does Job mean when he says, “mine hope hath he removed like a tree”?

answers: He cries out about wrong but is not heard and finds no judgment
He receives a clear judgment
He never calls upon God
challenge.explanation: Job says he cries out of wrong and cries aloud, but is not heard and finds no judgment.
challenge.q: How does Job present his situation before God?

answers: It presents a picture of security
It presents forces surrounding him and leaving him no escape
It describes Job’s journey
challenge.explanation: The troops around his tabernacle add to the image of siege, confinement, and helplessness.
challenge.q: How does the encampment around Job’s tabernacle reinforce the theme of obstruction?

paragraphs.title: The Withdrawal of Family and Society

answers: Only his neighbors
His brethren, acquaintances, relatives, and household members
Only his enemies
easy.explanation: Job names his brethren, acquaintance, kinsfolk, familiar friends, and those in his house.
easy.q: Who has become distant from Job?

answers: He gave no answer
He rescued Job
He invited Job into his house
easy.explanation: Job says, “I called my servant, and he gave me no answer.”
easy.q: How did Job’s servant respond when called?

answers: They honored him
They ignored him only
They despised him and spoke against him
easy.explanation: Job says that young children despised him and spoke against him when he arose.
easy.q: How did the young children treat Job?

answers: Relatives withdraw, household members treat him as a stranger, his servant ignores him, and others despise him
Family and friends gather to help him
Job’s social position rises
medium.explanation: The passage shows an expanding collapse of Job’s relationships and social support.
medium.q: What social progression is described in this passage?

answers: His acquaintances remembered him especially well
People who knew him had become distant from him
His acquaintances searched for him
medium.explanation: To be estranged is to be made distant or alienated from someone.
medium.q: What does “mine acquaintance are verily estranged from me” mean?

answers: They still regard him as a close master
They count him as a stranger and alien
They seek his counsel
medium.explanation: Job says that those in his house count him for a stranger and that he is an alien in their sight.
medium.q: What does the treatment by those in Job’s house reveal?

answers: It is limited to his immediate family
It includes relatives, acquaintances, household members, his servant, his wife, young children, and former friends
It results only from his servant’s silence
challenge.explanation: Job lists many different groups who have withdrawn from him, ignored him, or turned against him.
challenge.q: How broad is Job’s loneliness in this passage?

answers: His closest relationships have become hostile
He has found new friends
He has stopped loving everyone
challenge.explanation: The statement emphasizes the depth of Job’s betrayal and social abandonment.
challenge.q: What is emphasized by the statement that those Job loved are turned against him?

answers: Job seeks communication and mercy, but those around him reject or despise him
Job seeks control, and everyone obeys him
Job remains silent, and everyone praises him
challenge.explanation: Job calls his servant and pleads with others, yet he is met with rejection, silence, and contempt.
challenge.q: What contrast appears between Job’s actions and the response of those around him?

paragraphs.title: Physical Suffering and a Plea for Mercy

answers: As strong and healthy
As nearly only skin and bones
As covered with armor
easy.explanation: Job says that his bone cleaves to his skin and flesh and that he has escaped with the skin of his teeth.
easy.q: How does Job describe his body?

answers: His friends
His servant
His enemies
easy.explanation: Job pleads with his friends, saying, “Have pity upon me, have pity upon me.”
easy.q: From whom does Job ask for pity?

answers: It has not touched him
It has touched him
It has healed him
easy.explanation: Job says, “the hand of God hath touched me.”
easy.q: What does Job say about the hand of God?

answers: He is already suffering greatly and cannot bear their added persecution
He wants to leave his country
He wants them to give him possessions
medium.explanation: Job’s physical suffering and his friends’ treatment together lead him to plead for mercy.
medium.q: Why does Job ask his friends to stop persecuting him?

answers: He has survived by the narrowest margin and with almost nothing
He received a new garment
He fled to his friends’ house
medium.explanation: The expression pictures extremely narrow survival and desperate poverty.
medium.q: What does the expression “escaped with the skin of my teeth” communicate?

answers: His bodily suffering explains why he asks his friends for compassion
His health proves he needs no help
The two ideas are unrelated
medium.explanation: Job presents his emaciated condition as evidence of the mercy he urgently needs.
medium.q: How are Job’s physical condition and his plea for pity connected?

answers: They fail to recognize his suffering and add to it by persecuting him
They refuse to give him gifts
They will not discuss his family
challenge.explanation: Job asks them to see his suffering and stop treating him as though his persecution were justified.
challenge.q: What is the main point of Job’s protest against his friends?

answers: Together they describe the bodily affliction Job has endured
The first describes joy and the second a journey
They have no connection
challenge.explanation: Job’s damaged body and the hand of God are both part of his description of severe affliction.
challenge.q: How do the references to Job’s skin and flesh relate to the hand of God?

answers: A human response of compassion
A harsher judgment
Complete indifference
challenge.explanation: The repeated plea, “Have pity upon me,” is a direct request for mercy.
challenge.q: What does Job ask from his friends beyond intellectual understanding?

paragraphs.title: The Wish for Remembrance and Hope in a Living Redeemer

answers: That they would be forgotten immediately
That they would be written and preserved forever
That they would be given only to his servant
easy.explanation: Job wishes that his words would be written in a book and engraved in the rock forever.
easy.q: What does Job wish would happen to his words?

answers: That his redeemer lives
That his redeemer does not exist
That his redeemer is his friend
easy.explanation: Job declares, “I know that my redeemer liveth.”
easy.q: What does Job know about his redeemer?

answers: Only through hearsay
With his own eyes
Through the words of his friends
easy.explanation: Job says that his own eyes shall behold God and not another.
easy.q: How does Job expect to see God?

answers: So that they will endure and not be erased
So that they can be hidden
So that they can be used to build a house
medium.explanation: Writing in a book and engraving in rock express Job’s desire for lasting remembrance.
medium.q: Why does Job want his words engraved in rock?

answers: One who will stand for or vindicate him
One who drives him away
One who merely tells others about him
medium.explanation: Job presents his redeemer as a living advocate who will stand upon the earth for him.
medium.q: In this passage, what is a redeemer?

answers: Job wants his protest preserved while also expressing confidence that he will see God
Job abandons every hope
Job stops speaking about his suffering
medium.explanation: His desire to preserve his words stands alongside his declaration that his living redeemer will ultimately be seen.
medium.q: How do protest and hope function together in this passage?

answers: A personal and direct encounter with God
Seeing God through another person
An inability to see
challenge.explanation: Job stresses that he himself, rather than a substitute, will behold God.
challenge.q: What does “mine eyes shall behold, and not another” emphasize?

answers: From preserving a written testimony to expecting a future encounter with God
From describing his family to describing his servant
From sorrow to a celebration
challenge.explanation: Job first seeks to preserve his words and then turns to his hope of seeing God.
challenge.q: What is the major movement within this passage?

answers: It presents the redeemer as a living reality rather than merely a memory
It removes the possibility of seeing God
It describes the weakness of Job’s body
challenge.explanation: The word “liveth” gives substance and certainty to Job’s hope in his redeemer.
challenge.q: How does “I know that my redeemer liveth” strengthen Job’s hope?

paragraphs.title: A Warning to the Friends About Judgment

answers: The sword and judgment
Hunger only
A long journey
easy.explanation: Job tells them to be afraid of the sword and reminds them that there is a judgment.
easy.q: What does Job warn his friends about?

answers: That they have found the root of the matter in Job with certainty
That they should help him
That Job is entirely innocent by their own reasoning
easy.explanation: The question, “seeing the root of the matter is found in me,” reflects their assumption that Job’s guilt explains his suffering.
easy.q: What assumption do Job’s friends appear to be making?

answers: That there is a judgment
That their actions have no consequences
That they have nothing to fear
easy.explanation: Job says that the punishments of the sword should make them know there is a judgment.
easy.q: What must the friends know according to the final verse?

answers: They are judging him on an assumption rather than truly knowing his condition
They refuse to speak with him at all
They ask him for advice
medium.explanation: Job warns them that their confident judgment of him may itself bring consequences.
medium.q: Why does Job warn his friends about judgment?

answers: Be warned and take heed of judgment
Rejoice in the sword
Come closer to Job
medium.explanation: The command is a warning to fear the consequences associated with judgment.
medium.q: What does “Be ye afraid of the sword” mean in context?

answers: It exposes the friends’ assumption that Job’s supposed guilt justifies persecuting him
It describes Job’s desire to flee
It cancels the friends’ arguments
medium.explanation: Job presents their reasoning as though finding guilt in him would make persecution acceptable.
medium.q: How does the question “Why persecute we him?” relate to Job’s warning?

answers: Those who judge unjustly may themselves be judged
Only the sufferer bears responsibility
Judgment has no connection with conduct
challenge.explanation: Job reminds his friends that they too are accountable for the way they have judged him.
challenge.q: What moral principle emerges from Job’s warning?

answers: They act like judges while forgetting that they themselves are subject to judgment
They show mercy while Job threatens them without cause
They remain silent while Job asks them to speak
challenge.explanation: Job turns the issue of accountability back toward the friends who have condemned him.
challenge.q: What contrast appears between the friends’ behavior and Job’s final warning?

answers: After describing injustice and persecution, Job warns that persecution is not without responsibility
It returns only to the description of his body
It cancels his hope in the redeemer
challenge.explanation: The conclusion summarizes Job’s protest and reminds his friends that their treatment of him will also be judged.
challenge.q: How does the ending connect with the chapter as a whole?
